In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of an efficient and robust mathematical modeling of the fatigue behavior of concrete subjected to cyclic loading under uniaxial compressive loading conditions, which can be used in the context of numerical analysis.
the development of a novel fatigue model of plain concrete under compression based on the microplane theory.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model can capture the main aspects of the experimental behavior of plain concrete under compressive fatigue loading with an acceptable accuracy.
the proposed model is able to capture in a satisfactory way the fundamental inelastic behavior of concrete under compression with a consistent set of material properties.
the proposed model MS1 is capable to capture the main inelastic phenomena that occur in concrete subjected to fatigue loading under compression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a model for fatigue of concrete under compression can be developed within the microplane theory based on the principle on energy equivalence and a direct tensorial description of the effective elastic properties of the material.

the present model can be considered a promising tool for the analysis of the fatigue behavior of concrete structures under compressive loading, including the assessment of the fatigue life of structures.
the model can capture the fundamental mechanisms that govern the fatigue damage evolution in concrete and it can be used for the prediction of the fatigue response of concrete under compression.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the proposed model can capture the fatigue behavior of plain concrete under compression by using a simple and physically motivated damage evolution law that is based on the concept of cumulative inelastic shear strains.
fatigue damage in concrete under compression is mainly driven by inelastic shear/sliding between concrete aggregates.
the proposed microplane fatigue model is capable of reflecting the inelastic mechanisms that are responsible for the accumulation of damage at subcritical load ranges.
